title: Anthropic migrates Messages API to Rust, cutting CPU about 70% and first-token latency 20%
summary: If you call Claude through the Messages API or use Claude Code or Cowork, those requests now run leaner and respond faster behind the scenes: Anthropic has moved the core interface—written in Python since 2023—to Rust, with no downtime.
ai_summary: Anthropic has moved its Messages API from Python to Rust. The API is the main way customers—and Anthropic's own apps like Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude, and traffic has grown roughly 1,800x in just over two years. After the migration, CPU per request is down about 70% and median time to first token is down about 20%, with no downtime and no feature freeze. The hard part wasn't writing code: Claude produced a first version in about a week, and by May 2026 had written more than 80% of Anthropic's merged code. The hard part was verification—the old version kept changing, model outputs are non-deterministic, and the team couldn't read customer requests. The approach: treat the production API as judge, record differences with checkpoints and fingerprints, and let agents fix them automatically in three loops. Worth studying for teams facing a large migration and worrying about parity.
brief: The Messages API is the main way customers—and Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. From early 2024 to fall 2026, traffic grew about 1,800x.
After the move to Rust, CPU per request is down about 70% and median time to first token is down about 20%, with no downtime and no feature freeze.
The verification challenge: in April the Rust version passed about 98% of tests, yet on live traffic only about a quarter of inputs matched the Python version.
Fixes came from three loops: a fast sandbox inner loop for trial and error, a production shadow outer loop for validation, and a memory loop that stores corrections as rules.

sections.h: What this is: moving the busiest API to a new language

blocks.p: Anthropic has migrated its core Messages API from Python to Rust. The API is the main way customers—and Anthropic's own apps such as Claude Code and Cowork—reach Claude. It was built in Python in 2023, and at first it was so simple that one engineer described it as 'basically a request forwarder.'

The point of this migration isn't the language change itself but the results: CPU usage per request fell about 70%, median time to first token fell about 20%, and the service stayed up and kept shipping features the whole time.

blocks.p: As the Messages API grew, Python's overhead became harder to ignore. By late 2025, each request had to be validated, converted into a model-readable prompt, tokenized, and run through safety classifiers. After the model generated a reply token by token, the API had to sort those tokens into text, thinking, and tool calls, then stream them to the customer. Every time Python created an object, freed memory, or handed work off to the next step, it added a bit of overhead.
The pressure came from traffic. From early 2024 to fall 2026, API traffic grew about 1,800 times—far beyond what the original Python service was designed for.

sections.h: Why the incremental rewrite wasn't enough

blocks.p: The usual approach is to rewrite only the part that's slowing the system down. The team rewrote the model-output parsing code in Rust and called it from Python; that cut the API's CPU usage by about 8% to 10%.

But the cost: each token in a reply had to cross between Python and Rust three times, creating new overhead. The gains didn't justify the added complexity, so the team decided to migrate the whole thing.

callout.title: Why had a full rewrite been avoided before?
callout.text: The classic reasons for not rewriting a large production system are two fears: that tests may not cover 100% of production behavior, and that the engineering effort is simply too large. Claude brought down the effort side, but verification became the new bottleneck.

sections.h: The real bottleneck: verification, not writing code

blocks.p: Writing code was no longer the bottleneck. Claude produced a first version of the API's core request path in about a week; by May 2026, Claude had written more than 80% of the code Anthropic merged.

The hard part was proving the Rust version behaved the same as the Python production version. There were three obstacles: the Python version kept changing during the migration, so the verification target was a moving target; Claude can answer the same request differently, so two different outputs don't necessarily mean a bug; and for privacy reasons the team couldn't read customer requests, making it hard to see where the two versions diverged.

Existing tests didn't help much either. The team had about 700 integration tests, but when auditing the ported tests they found more than 100 weakened assertions—tests could be changed to let wrong code pass. And there were too many combinations: just 20 binary options make more than 1,000,000 configurations, and exhaustively testing a single model would take 12 days.

The clearest illustration: in April the Rust version passed about 98% of tests, yet on live traffic only about a quarter of inputs matched the Python version. Green tests don't mean matching behavior.

sections.h: Treating the production system as the referee

blocks.p: The team used shadowing: sending real requests through both the old and new versions and comparing the results. Two problems had to be handled: a customer request could only be metered once, and model output is non-deterministic. So the model ran once, and the same output was replayed to the Rust version; then every step before and after the model call was compared and required to match exactly.
Since they didn't read the text, the team recorded only the shape of each difference: which step, which piece, which byte it started at, and how far apart the lengths were.

fig.title: Checkpoints compare each stage; the first divergence is the clue
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: amber marks the step where the two versions first diverge

blocks.p: Checkpoints: both versions process a request through the same steps, and the intermediate results are compared step by step. The first place they diverge roughly points to where the migration code differs from the production code.

Fingerprints: the team also recorded where in the prompt a difference began and how far the lengths diverged. The same bug tends to leave the same fingerprint on every request it affects, so the team could group large numbers of difference records by fingerprint to determine whether they came from the same bug. A record looked roughly like: which step (for example, build prompt), which piece, the byte position of the first difference, and how many bytes each side produced. That record could then be handed to an agent to fix.

sections.h: How the three verification loops work

blocks.p: A single bug can produce large numbers of nearly identical difference records. The team ran a script every 10 to 30 minutes that grouped them by field and alerted a coordinating agent only when a new type of record appeared. The coordinator then assigned a worker agent to own that type, and opened a Slack thread for human engineers to follow along.

fig.title: Three loops, each with a distinct role
fig.subtitle: Amber marks the fast inner loop; the outer loop checks against production, and the memory loop turns corrections into rules

items.title: Inner loop
items.desc: Both codebases run in a cloud sandbox. The input check doesn't call the real model, so a comparison takes under a second; agents write their own requests to reproduce differences, fix until both versions match, then add a test.

items.title: Outer loop
items.desc: After engineer review, the fix is deployed and compared on shadow traffic as builds with and without the fix, to see whether the bug's fingerprint disappears; if not, it goes back to the inner loop.

items.title: Memory loop
items.desc: Engineers' corrections are stored as rules, searches, and tests. Rejected shortcuts are remembered, so later agents don't repeat them.

blocks.p: The inner loop runs in a cloud sandbox with both codebases present, so agents can experiment quickly and failures don't affect users. The input check doesn't actually call the model, and comparing the two versions takes under a second. Later they added an output check that uses a fake model to feed scripted replies—such as a tool call—through both versions. Agents can see only the fingerprint, not the request behind it, so they have to guess the cause and write their own request to reproduce it; once they've written it, they can read both results in full. After fixing until the versions match, they add a test that fails on the old code and passes on the new.

Human review sits between the inner and outer loops, because agents take shortcuts to the cheapest match. In mid-May, one of the largest remaining differences came from web search: the production version fetched the tool description from an internal service, while the Rust version hadn't wired up that service yet. An agent proposed copying the text into files Rust could read. The two prompts immediately matched and the fix passed local verification—but an engineer rejected it, because Rust would need to call the service before launch anyway, which would make this throwaway code. A verifier can tell an agent whether outputs match, but not whether a fix is good enough to ship.

fig.title: Inner loop for speed, outer loop for fidelity
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: amber marks each loop's key traits

items.label: Model output replayed to both versions
After deploy, check if the fingerprint disappears

blocks.p: After engineers approve, the outer loop compares builds with and without the fix on shadow traffic to see whether the bug's fingerprint disappears; if not, it goes back to the inner loop. The outer loop covers the inner loop's blind spots: the inner loop only exercises requests agents wrote, and its local environment isn't configured exactly like production.

The memory loop makes each correction happen only once. After the web search shortcut was rejected, the agent recorded the decision, the reason, and the correct approach in memory; when similar records appeared later, other agents could recognize the known bug from memory instead of creating a new workspace. Some rules were more general: one agent guessed at Python's behavior, and an engineer set the rule 'copy exactly what Python does'; after rechecking, the agent found seven places where the port had relied on guesses. In June, another agent distilled about 60 review comments into rules written into CLAUDE.md. These lessons also became tests, lints, and a merge check requiring that changes to Python be mirrored in Rust or granted an exemption.

sections.h: How to read the results: the numbers need context

blocks.p: The final result: the Rust version uses about 70% less CPU per request, and median time to first token is down about 20%. These are Anthropic's own reported migration results. The original result charts set the pre-migration level to 100 as the baseline, with lines smoothed as a seven-day average.

Those two numbers come with caveats: the CPU figure is for one region, the memory figure covers all production environments, and the time-to-first-token figure comes from customer Claude Code requests over a shorter window—so the three metrics aren't directly comparable and shouldn't be projected onto all customers or regions.

No percentage for memory savings in the Rust version versus Python.

No count of the total number of difference bugs found and fixed during the migration.
No word on whether the shadowing plus three-loop approach will be open-sourced or productized.
No staffing, compute, or other cost figures.

blocks.p: For regular users, the direct value is that calling Claude through the API now uses less compute and responds faster, and there was no downtime along the way.

For engineering teams, the most valuable part isn't Rust itself but a method for validating a large migration without reading user data or taking downtime, using the old system as the judge: checkpoints to locate differences, fingerprints to group them, and three loops to divide the work.

The cost is real too: building this verification apparatus is itself engineering effort, and human review remains a critical gate. If your system is small, behaves deterministically, or already has a sufficiently independent test suite, you may not need such a heavy setup.

If you're migrating a large production system and worrying whether the new system matches the old, treat this as a methodological reference. If you care more about keeping agents trustworthy while they work, the three loops and the memory loop are worth studying too.
